title: Train, Validation & Test Sets
html:
You can't measure generalisation on the data you trained on. Hold data back: a validation set to make choices and a test set, used once, to report how the final model will do on new data.

SplitUsed forTypical share
TrainingFitting parameters (fit)60–80%
ValidationChoosing hyperparameters, features, the model, the decision threshold; early stopping10–20% (or cross-validation instead)
TestOne final, unbiased estimate of performance — after all decisions are made10–20%

The shares are rules of thumb. With millions of rows, 1% can be a perfectly large test set; with a few hundred rows, prefer cross-validation for model selection and keep a small test set — or use nested cross-validation.

A three-way split

Why stratify

With a rare class, a purely random split can leave the test set with almost no positives. stratify=y keeps the class proportions identical in every split:

When a random split is wrong

DataProblem with a random splitSplit instead by
Time-ordered (sales, prices, logs)Training on the future to predict the pastTime: train on earlier, validate/test on later
Grouped (several rows per patient, user, device)The model recognises the entity, not the patternGroup: all rows of an entity in one split
Near-duplicates (same image resized, reposted listings)Test rows are copies of training rowsDeduplicate first, or group duplicates

Rules that keep evaluation honest

  1. Split first, before fitting any imputer, scaler, encoder or feature selector.
  2. Fit everything on the training data; only transform the validation and test data.
  3. Make every decision with validation data or cross-validation.
  4. Look at the test set once. If you then change the model because of it, it has become a validation set and its score is optimistic.
  5. After choosing the model, refit it on train + validation before deploying (more data, same recipe).

Reading the gaps

Training errorValidation errorDiagnosisNext step
HighHigh (similar)Underfitting (high bias)More capacity, better features, less regularisation
LowMuch higherOverfitting (high variance)More data, regularisation, simpler model, early stopping
LowLowGood fitConfirm on the test set

See Bias–Variance & Overfitting for the theory and learning curves.

Why do we need a validation set in addition to a test set?

Every choice made by comparing scores — hyperparameters, features, models — fits the data those scores came from. If you make them on the test set, the test score becomes optimistically biased. The validation set absorbs that selection bias; the untouched test set then gives an honest final estimate.

You tuned on the test set by mistake. What now?

Treat that score as a validation score, not a generalisation estimate. Get a fresh held-out set (new data, or a later time period) for the final evaluation, and switch to cross-validation for tuning.
